title: Oertel’s mixed-integer centerpoint conjecture
formal: For all integers n,d≥0 with n+d≥1 and every compact convex body \(C\subset\mathbb R^{n+d}\) with nonempty interior and positive mixed-integer volume, is there \(y\in C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\) such that every closed halfspace H containing y satisfies \(\mu_C(H)\ge\mu_C(\mathbb R^{n+d})/(2^n e)\)?
definitions: For a Borel set B in the ambient space, define \[\mu_C(B)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\operatorname{vol}_d\{u\in\mathbb R^d:(z,u)\in C\cap B\}.\]Here vol_d is d-dimensional Lebesgue measure; vol_0 assigns mass one to the singleton R^0. For n=0 the sum has one summand. Compactness ensures only finitely many integer fibers contribute and total volume is finite; positivity is assumed. A closed halfspace has the form \(H=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle\ge b\}\) for a nonzero real vector a and real b. The number e is the base of the natural logarithm. The center y must itself have integral first n coordinates. No lower bound on projection width or on an inscribed ball is assumed, and no algorithm for finding y is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof for all dimensions and bodies, or a counterexample in which every allowed center belongs to a halfspace capturing strictly less than the proposed fraction. A proof restricted to sufficiently thick projections does not settle the unrestricted conjecture.
context:
Mixed-integer centerpoints extend volumetric depth to a measure summed over integer fibers and support cutting-plane complexity bounds.

The 2026 theorem verifies the conjecture under a quantitative thickness assumption on the integer-coordinate projection, not for every body.
why: A universal mixed-integer centerpoint guarantee would link convex geometry to progress bounds for cutting-plane optimization.

import_provenance.original_statement: For a convex body C in R^{n+d}, must C∩(Z^n×R^d) contain a point such that every closed halfspace containing it captures at least 1/(2^n e) of the total mixed-integer volume? Volume here sums d-dimensional volumes over integer fibers; the conjecture controls progress guarantees for mixed-integer cutting-plane optimization.

sentences: Volume is summed over fibers whose first coordinates are integers.
A center must lie on one of those mixed-integer fibers.
Every halfspace through the center must retain a specified fraction of the total measure.
The target imposes no thickness assumption on the body.
Recent progress proves a larger thickness-qualified family but leaves the full claim.
